_FileSystemIdentity_comment: Every request through the access point is authorized as this one file system identity, so
callers are indistinguishable from each other through it. Restriction lives in two places, and
both apply: an explicit Deny in the access point policy on the AWS side, and the file
permissions this identity holds on the volume. Narrowing the Allow is not a restriction --
within one account the caller's identity policy can grant the action on its own.
Measured in the sibling repository: with no access point policy attached at all, changing only
the volume root's uid/gid/mode bits flipped PutObject between AccessDenied and success. So file
permissions do gate access, and they are the harder of the two to bypass.
The name below is not root on purpose. All requests carry this one identity, so root (uid 0)
removes the file-permission layer entirely. Create the user on the SVM first and give it
ownership of the target directory. FileSystemIdentity cannot be changed after creation, so a
read-only consumer and a writer need separate access points.
Being non-root is not itself the control. What settles whether this identity can write is the
effective permission it holds on the volume root, so a non-root identity that owns the root
writes freely -- which is what this example arranges, because it is a writer. Give it ownership
of the target directory before creating the access point.
For a read-only access point, the identity has to be one the volume root grants no write to.
That was measured in the sibling repository: with no policy attached, a non-root identity
served GetObject and was denied PutObject, where the volume was 755 and the identity was
neither its owner nor in its owning group. **The mode bits are part of that claim.** At 775 or
777, or with the identity as owner, the same non-root identity writes. So a read-only access
point needs both decided: an identity the volume withholds write from, and -- for defence in
depth, so one misconfiguration does not open it -- an explicit Deny in the access point policy.
Which layer denied a request is readable from the error body: an unqualified `Access Denied` is
Layer 2 and no policy explains it; `with an explicit deny in a resource-based policy` is a Deny
in Layer 1; `because no identity-based policy allows the s3:... action` is Layer 1 with nothing
granting it.
The API takes a user *name*, not a uid/gid pair (OntapUnixFileSystemUser has a single Name
field). UNIX pairs with a UNIX security style volume and NFS on the fan-out side; for NTFS and
SMB use a WINDOWS identity. Joining the SVM to Active Directory is not required for either --
a workgroup-mode CIFS server with local users is documented and was measured. But on an
AD-joined SVM every data operation through the access point needs a reachable domain
controller, and HeadBucket still succeeds when it is unreachable, so it cannot check that.
Delete the _comment keys before use.

_NetworkOrigin_comment: Immutable after creation. VPC restricts the access point to a VPC; Internet makes it reachable
from outside the VPC as well. Reachability is decided by where the caller is and how it is
routed, not by the origin type: a caller inside the VPC needs an S3 VPC endpoint whose route
is associated with its subnet, and a caller arriving over VPN, Direct Connect, a peered VPC or
Transit Gateway needs an Interface endpoint, because a Gateway endpoint only routes traffic
For a single-host measurement, VPC with the verification host's VPC keeps the write and the
read on one clock and off the public internet. Replace the whole VpcConfiguration block with
"NetworkOrigin": "Internet" only if you need to write from outside.
